transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Some House and Senate races
from Tuesday's midterm elections have yet to be called.
They include Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi.
In Mississippi, Democratic nominee Scott Colom
holds a small lead over
rather Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde Smith.
Elise Katrina Gregg of the Gulf States Newsroom
and Mississippi Public Broadcasting has more.
Mississippi doesn't have runoffs or recounts
for U.S. Senate races,
so small swings in the ballot count
could make or break either candidate.
Both candidates say they're confident they'll win.
Here's Colom addressing supporters.
Confident once the process lays out where we are,
where the ballots are, we're gonna win.
We're gonna win.
And it's because the people of Mississippi
turned out in historic numbers
to make this race possible in a midterm election.
Local officials in the Jackson area
say it could take several days to count remaining ballots.
For NPR News, I'm Elise Katrina Gregg in Jackson.
Democrats flipped at least seven seats in the Senate
and more than two dozen House seats in the election.
They will retake control of Congress
from Republicans in January.
In Alaska's Senate race, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola
holds a very small lead over Republican incumbent
Dan Sullivan.
That may take a couple more weeks to determine the winner.
Democrats who are getting ready to come to Congress
next year are setting their goals.
And BRSam Greenglass says they intend to launch
very quickly.
In the first hundred hours Democrats wanna restore
enhanced ACA health subsidies, reverse Medicaid cuts
that Republicans passed last year,
reassert Congress's prerogative over tariffs
and try to force an end to the war with Iran.
All priorities Democrats have near total consensus on.
NPR's Sam Greenglass reporting.
Bomb threats disrupted flights across Europe today,
forced emergency landings and diversions
for the second time this week.
Meghan Williams has the latest from Rome.
Italian fighter jets escorted a passenger plane arriving
here in Rome from Finland after a bomb threat
and French fighter jets escorted another Rome bound flight
from Dublin to a military air base west of Paris.
Similar threats have disrupted flights across Europe
from Belgium to Bulgaria, triggering emergency landings,
evacuations and security searches.
Anonymous emails reportedly carried the threats.
Earlier this week, bomb threats targeted
at least seven flights and a cruise ship
with no explosives found.
European officials have accused Russia and Iran
of conducting campaigns to sow chaos,
but there's no evidence linking either country
to those threats so far.
For NPR News, I'm Meghan Williams in Rome.
This is NPR.
The White House says First Lady Melania Trump
will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine today.
They're supposed to discuss a recent ceasefire
she helped broker in a Ukrainian town near the front line.
Hundreds of civilians were able to leave
for other parts of Ukraine or for Russia.
Mrs. Trump's effort comes ahead
of U.S.-led peace talks next week.
South Korea is planning to expand its naval mission
in the Middle East to include waters
near the Strait of Hormuz.
And there's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul.
South Korea insists it will not be drawn
into the war between the U.S. and Iran.
The South Korean Navy's Chonghe unit
has conducted anti-piracy missions
in the Gulf of Aden since 2009.
Its mission will be extended for another year,
and its area will be expanded to within about 400 miles
of the Strait of Hormuz.
President Trump complained that Seoul had not contributed
to the war in Iran when he scaled back
U.S.-South Korean military drills in August,
aimed at deterring North Korea.
South Korea gets most of its oil
through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Chonghe unit's extended deployment
is subject to parliamentary approval,
and Seoul has made clear that its mission
is to protect South Korean interests
and will not involve any combat operations.
Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
The National Weather Service says catastrophic flooding
is happening this morning in parts
of southeastern Tennessee and northern Georgia.
Cars and buildings are inundated.
Authorities in the area are rescuing trapped people
from floodwaters.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.
So...

topics.text: Mississippi Senate race between Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde Smith too close to call
Alaska Senate race between Mary Peltola and Dan Sullivan still undecided after Tuesday's midterms
Democrats outline first-hundred-hours agenda on ACA subsidies, Medicaid, tariffs, and Iran war
Bomb threats force flight diversions and emergency landings across Europe, including Rome and Paris
Melania Trump to host Russian and Ukrainian representatives on ceasefire in Ukrainian front-line town
South Korea plans to extend naval anti-piracy mission near Strait of Hormuz for another year
Catastrophic flooding hits southeastern Tennessee and northern Georgia, with people trapped by floodwaters
